Yesterday we learned to describe a dataset. Today we will start asking questions of it.

Day 3 brings in two new patterns that address most of the questions anyone asks of a
table. We begin this morning with booleans, comparison operators and `if`/`elif`/`else`,
because they are the underlying grammar that a filter depends on. The **filter pattern**,
which allows you to keep the rows that satisfy a condition, follows in the second session of
the morning. Then this afternoon we take up the **top-N pattern**, which puts the rows in
order and takes the first few from the front of the list. The N is a stand-in for however
many rows you want back, so you write `.head(10)` when you want the top ten and `.head(3)`
when you want the top three.

## End-of-day practice

Later today you will rank the foods in *The Economist*'s banana index, which scores the carbon
emissions of a food against those of a banana. You will rank them three ways: per kilogram of food,
per thousand calories, and per hundred grams of protein. The three rankings disagree with each
other, and working out why is most of the practice.

- [{{< fa pencil title="A pencil" >}} **Day 3 Practice:** The Banana Index](eod-practice/eod-day3-2026.qmd)
